title: Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80
dek: Dolly Parton, the country music legend who rose from poverty in East Tennessee to build a global entertainment and business empire, died Tuesday, August 25, 2026, at age 80 after a brief battle with cancer. Her nephew announced the death via video on her Instagram account. Parton sold over 100 million records, won 11 Grammy Awards, and was tied for the most Grammy nominations at 46.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Dolly Parton died on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, at age 80 at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones after a brief battle with cancer.
bottom_line: Parton's death marks the end of a career spanning more than six decades that reshaped American country music and extended into global entertainment, business, and philanthropy. Her legacy as a songwriter, performer, businesswoman, and advocate for social acceptance will continue to be assessed in the weeks and months ahead.
body: Dolly Parton, the country music legend and global entertainment figure, died Tuesday, August 25, 2026, at age 80. According to ABC News, she died at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones after a brief battle with cancer. Her nephew, Brian Seaver, announced the death in a video posted on her Instagram account.

Parton rose from a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River near Sevierville, Tennessee, to build a career that transcended music into film, business, and philanthropy. Born January 19, 1946, the fourth of 12 children to parents Robert Lee Parton and Avie Lee Parton, she became one of the most prolific artists in American entertainment history.

During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records, according to NBC News. She won 11 Grammy Awards and is tied for the most Grammy nominations at 46, per ABC News. In 2014, the Record Industry Association of America recognized her for sales of over 100 million units worldwide, including 19 RIAA-certified gold, platinum, and multi-platinum albums across more than 100 studio, live, and compilation albums. Her estimated net worth was placed at 650 million dollars by her team, though Forbes magazine in June 2025 estimated it at 450 million dollars, placing her number 78 on their list of America's wealthiest self-made women.

Parton's songwriting and performances shaped popular music globally. Per ABC News, she wrote and recorded enduring songs including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "Love Is Like a Butterfly," and "9 to 5," for which she wrote both the song and performed the theme for the 1980 film of that name, opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. The song became a chart-topper and won a Grammy Award. Her most famous composition, "I Will Always Love You," topped the charts three times; Whitney Houston's 1992 cover became a global smash and remains the best-selling song by a female artist of all time. According to ABC News, "Coat of Many Colors" was added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2011.

Beyond music, Parton appeared in approximately nine films, not including cameos as herself, according to ABC News. Her big-screen debut came in the 1980 hit comedy "9 to 5," and she later appeared in the 1989 comedy-drama "Steel Magnolias." She presided over an entertainment empire that included Dollywood, her Tennessee theme park, and through the Dollywood Foundation, she launched programs providing poverty relief and funding educational initiatives in her native East Tennessee.

Parton married Carl Dean in 1966. Dean died in March 2025 at age 82. In July 2025, per NBC News, Parton told People magazine: "Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years." In recent months, Parton acknowledged health struggles. She announced in May that she was canceling a Las Vegas show and had been undergoing treatment for kidney stones for several years. In September 2025, she stated her doctors had told her she required procedures, though she did not specify their nature. Ten days before her death, she canceled a scheduled appearance at Dollywood, saying her doctor had advised against travel due to health issues. On Friday before her death, per NBC News, she acknowledged she had lost a step following her husband's passing but told People magazine: "Even though I'm still healin', I'm still workin'! You know me—as I've often said—I've dreamed myself into a corner, and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I'm gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life."

Parton was publicly vocal on social issues. In a 2017 interview with Larry King, per NBC News, she said: "I keep saying: If you're the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people. That's God's job." She told a British outlet, per NBC News: "I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals." In her 2023 book "Behind the Seams: My Life in Rhinestones," per ABC News, she wrote: "I take my negatives and try to make them into positives, and I always feel better being more flamboyant. Maybe I looked cheap, but I knew I wasn't cheap." She was famous for the quote: "It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."

Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, said in a video statement, per ABC News: "By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history." Seaver also shared that Parton told him "she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

President Donald Trump ordered U.S. flags lowered to half-staff nationwide for one week. According to ABC News, Trump stated: "There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM."
